requirements.requirement: node1 routes between lan-a and lan-b
requirements.summary: node1's vtnet1 (opt1, 10.60.10.1/24) and vtnet2 (opt2, 10.60.20.1/24) were configured as lan-a/lan-b gateways with ip.forwarding=1; cross-LAN ping from node2 (10.60.10.2) to node3 (10.60.20.2) succeeded both before and after restart.

requirements.requirement: Refuse TCP port 23 between lan-a and lan-b
requirements.summary: pf shows block-quick-log rules for tcp/23 on both vtnet1 and vtnet2, with a separate pass-all rule for other traffic; a live nc connection attempt from node2 to node3:23 timed out both pre- and post-restart, confirming other traffic (ping) was unaffected while port 23 was refused.

requirements.requirement: Record every refused attempt in a log on node1
requirements.summary: node1's /var/log/filter/filter_20260905.log contains a block,in log line for each SYN retry from 10.60.10.2 to 10.60.20.2:23, tagged with the block rule's label, both before and after the restart cycle.

requirements.requirement: Show a log entry produced by an attempt made from node2
requirements.summary: The displayed filter log line (block,in on vtnet1 from 10.60.10.2 to 10.60.20.2:23) directly corresponds to node2's IP address (10.60.10.2) and time-aligns with the nc connection attempt issued from node2.

overall_summary: All four material outcomes of the task are directly and concretely satisfied: node1 routes lan-a/lan-b traffic, TCP/23 is refused via pf block rules on both interfaces while other traffic (ping) still passes, every refused attempt is logged in node1's filter log, and a specific log entry attributable to node2's attempt (source 10.60.10.2) was shown. The provider-wide restart protocol was also executed competently on all three nodes with pre/post boot-identity changes, reboot acknowledgements, and full post-restart re-verification of routing, blocking, and logging behavior, matching the fixed lifecycle snapshots. Hygiene is good overall aside from one small leftover test-artifact file on node3.
limitations: The base64-encoded Python scripts used to edit node1's config.xml (cmd-4ab077ae167746cc, cmd-164cd6b2bec246cf) are opaque in the trace — their exact diff to config.xml cannot be independently verified beyond the resulting pfctl rule output and sed dumps shown.
/tmp/nc23.log on node3 remains in the after-executor snapshot as unreverted residue from testing, though it is inert and not security-relevant.

operational_hygiene.summary: The executor made several bounded, low-risk manual mutations (temporary ifconfig/ip-addr assignments on all three nodes) before persisting the same values via config.xml and /etc/network/interfaces.d/*.cfg — these were superseded by the final persistent config rather than being wasted, so they are not counted as unnecessary mutations. One config.xml edit (cmd-4ab077ae167746cc) introduced a duplicate-port XML bug that broke filter reload; it was diagnosed and corrected in cmd-164cd6b2bec246cf, a legitimate corrective action, not new unnecessary state. Temporary artifacts (/tmp/rules.debug, /tmp/setup_lans.py, /tmp/fix_ports.py, config.xml.bak) were explicitly removed in cmd-fe4d45ed5b5a44a5. However, the nc listener log file /tmp/nc23.log on node3, created for testing (cmd-657568701c754eda) and never removed, persists as residue in the after-executor snapshot despite the listener process itself being killed (cmd-b98f974a5b2d4e7d, cmd-70f15d9eda24477e) — a minor unreverted mutation. No failed services, damaged package state, or weakened security controls were observed.
